introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Writing and Analysis), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least one question from each section.

Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- Coherence and organization of material;
- Clear presentation of the problematic;
- Identification and development of the Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis and Conclusion as prescribed.

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR questions, choosing at least one question from each section » (quatre questions au total, au moins une par section). `regles_choix` porte le minimum, une règle `parmi 1 sur 2` par section (Section One : questions 1-2 ; Section Two : questions 3-4 ; Section Three : questions 5-6) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. Le sujet ne dit pas si un candidat peut traiter les deux questions de la Section Three.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les critères de la page de garde (cohérence et organisation, présentation claire de la problématique, thèse, antithèse, synthèse et conclusion) s'appliquent aux dissertations (questions 1 à 4) sans barème chiffré par partie ; les questions de textes (5 et 6) ont leurs points par sous-question (Q5 : 5 + 4 + 6 + 6 + 4 = 25 ; Q6 : 5 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 25) : aucun écart de somme constaté, aucun point corrigé.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les auteurs et positions cités sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie établie, sans citation littérale, sans numéro de page et sans date ; à faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com / Kawlo sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy 2, Paper 2 (Philosophical Writing and Analysis), code 0790, JUNE 2023, trois heures.

Q3 : positions attribuées aux auteurs (Tempels, Kagame, Mbiti, Senghor, Gyekye, Oruka, Hallen et Sodipo ; critiques de Hountondji, Towa, Wiredu, Bodunrin, Eboussi Boulaga ; Lévy-Bruhl et Hegel) conformes à la classification courante de la philosophie africaine, en grandes lignes, sans citation littérale, sans titre d'ouvrage ni date. Le rattachement de Senghor à l'ethno-philosophie est discuté (« in a way » dans le corrigé) ; à faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction (problematic).** *Ethno-philosophy* names the study and presentation of the collective world-views of African peoples (their myths, proverbs, rituals, religious beliefs and customs) as a philosophy. Placide Tempels, Alexis Kagame, John Mbiti and in a way Léopold Senghor are among its best-known representatives, while Paulin Hountondji, Marcien Towa and Kwasi Wiredu are among its critics. The problem is whether this body of collective beliefs deserves the name of philosophy, that is, a critical, reasoned and rational discipline, or whether it is only ethnology and folklore.

**Thesis: ethno-philosophy is philosophical.**
- *Every culture has a philosophy.* Each people holds implicit answers to the basic questions: what exists, what a person is, what is good, what happens after death, how knowledge is gained. Tempels argued that Bantu thought forms a coherent ontology (being as vital force), Mbiti analysed African concepts of God, time and the person, and Kagame studied the categories of being embodied in the Kinyarwanda language. Kwame Gyekye stresses that a tradition is philosophical when its ideas can be analysed and defended by argument.
- *Denying it is Eurocentric.* The claim that Africans had no philosophy repeats the colonial view (Lévy-Bruhl's "prelogical mentality", Hegel's judgement on Africa). Ethno-philosophy was a reply that restored dignity to African thought and showed its rationality.
- *Philosophy begins in culture.* Greek philosophy also grew out of myth and common belief. If Western philosophy is allowed to begin in its own tradition, African philosophy may begin in African traditions.
- *Evidence of critical thought within the tradition.* Odera Oruka's work on "sage philosophy" shows that some members of traditional communities reason critically, question received beliefs and offer personal arguments. Hallen and Sodipo's study of Yoruba concepts of knowledge and belief treats oral thought as a field for conceptual analysis.

**Antithesis: ethno-philosophy is not philosophical as such.**
- *It is collective and unanimist.* Hountondji criticises the assumption that a whole people shares one system of thought ("unanimism"). Philosophy, he holds, requires individuals who argue and disagree; a description of beliefs is ethnology, not philosophy.
- *It lacks critical reflection.* Ethno-philosophy describes what people believe without asking whether the beliefs are true or justified. Wiredu and Bodunrin distinguish folk thought (a body of beliefs) from philosophy (a critical, argued discipline).
- *Its origin and audience.* Much of it was written by Europeans (Tempels was a missionary) or by Africans addressing Europeans, and used Western categories (such as "being") to interpret African languages. Towa and Eboussi Boulaga see in it an apologetic attempt to prove that Africans too have a philosophy, which neglects the real tasks of philosophy.
- *Political weakness.* By presenting tradition as a closed and unchanging whole, it can serve to avoid questioning present problems of development and freedom.

**Synthesis.** The two positions are partly reconciled by distinguishing the material from the method. Traditional beliefs, proverbs and myths are the raw material of African philosophy, and many are rich in philosophical content. They become philosophy when they are examined, interpreted, compared and justified by critical argument, as Wiredu's conceptual analysis, Gyekye's reflective study of communitarian thought and Oruka's sages show. Ethno-philosophy is therefore philosophical in a limited sense (it supplies problems and concepts) and not philosophical when it stops at description.

**Conclusion.** Ethno-philosophy is not philosophical in itself, but it is philosophically valuable as a starting point. The criticisms of Hountondji, Towa and Wiredu show that description of collective beliefs does not satisfy the standard of critical, argued thought; the defenders show that this tradition contains real philosophical problems and has answered the charge that Africans had no philosophy. An African philosophy worthy of the name takes up the tradition critically and does not simply repeat it.
